name: Spine
tagline: Desktop editor for rigging and animating 2D sprites with bones, meshes and runtimes for most game engines.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Spine sells perpetual licenses, not subscriptions, so a monthly figure is not meaningful.

verdictSummary: The math of 2D skeletal animation is not secret: parent transforms, keyframes, interpolation, a JSON file, a small playback runtime. An agent can absolutely produce a working bone editor with a timeline and an exporter in a weekend, and for a hobby project with cut-up PNG parts that is genuinely enough. What it will not produce is mesh deformation with weighted skinning, IK and transform constraints, physics, a curve editor you can stand to use for ten hours, and official runtimes for Unity, Unreal, Godot, Cocos, LibGDX, Phaser and friends. Spine's real product is the boring half: fifteen years of runtime maintenance across engine versions plus a UI that professional animators do not fight. You are cloning the fun 20 percent.
coreLoopDIY: Import sprite parts, build a bone hierarchy, pose and keyframe them on a timeline, export a JSON animation file, and play it back with a tiny canvas runtime you also own.
requirements: Sprite art already separated into individual PNG parts
A target engine you are willing to write and maintain a small runtime for
Comfort hand-editing a JSON format when the editor does not cover a case
whatYouLose: Mesh deformation and weighted skinning, which is where most of Spine's expressive range lives
IK, transform and path constraints, plus physics on bones
Official, tested runtimes for a dozen engines, kept working across engine upgrades
A timeline and curve editor that survives long animation sessions without rage
Interop: nobody else can open your format, and studio pipelines expect Spine JSON
moatNotes: The runtime matrix is the quiet moat. Writing one canvas player is a weekend; keeping seven engine runtimes correct for a decade is a company.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because animation tools are used for hundreds of hours and every rough edge compounds, and because shipping a game means the animation has to actually play in the engine you chose, on the version you are stuck on, at the framerate you promised. Spine is bought once, not rented, which makes the price argument mostly emotional. If you are a solo dev with paper-doll sprites, roll your own and enjoy owning the format. If you are animating a character with squash, stretch and mesh warping that someone else has to maintain, the license is cheaper than your weekend.
notes: Rare case where the paid thing is a one-time purchase, which quietly ruins most build-it-yourself math.
prompt:
Build "Bonewright", a local-only 2D skeletal animation editor that runs in the browser.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + TypeScript, Canvas 2D for the viewport, plain DOM for UI, no React, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no analytics. No .env needed because there are no secrets.

Editor requirements:
- Load sprite parts via a file input (multiple PNGs); each becomes an attachment in the asset list.
- Skeleton tree: create, rename, reparent and delete bones. Bone transform is translation, rotation, scale, with proper parent composition.
- Slots: attach a sprite to a bone with a local offset and draw order the user can reorder.
- Viewport: click to select a bone, drag to translate, modifier-drag to rotate, gizmo drawn as a line plus handle. Zoom and pan.
- Timeline: multiple named animations, per-bone keyframes on translate/rotate/scale channels, dopesheet rows, scrubbing, playback with loop, adjustable fps and duration.
- Interpolation per key: linear, stepped, and a cubic bezier with two draggable control points in a small curve panel.
- Setup pose vs animate mode, clearly toggled, so animation keys are deltas from setup pose.
- Undo/redo stack covering all edits.

Persistence and export:
- Autosave the project (skeleton, slots, animations, image blobs) to IndexedDB on every change.
- Export/import a single project .json plus an images folder as a .zip download.
- Export a documented runtime format: bones, slots, attachments, animations with keyframe arrays.

Also ship src/runtime/bonewright.ts: a dependency-free player under 300 lines that loads the exported JSON plus images and draws an animation onto any canvas, with a demo page proving it plays.

Explicitly out of scope, do not attempt: mesh deformation, weighted skinning, IK or physics constraints, Unity/Unreal/Godot exporters, multi-user editing.

Deliver a README with run instructions, the JSON format spec, and an honest list of what this does not do.
